```{r}
summary_table_percent <- function(cells, table_name, column_label, row_label, accuracy = 0.1) {
  cells %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      .data$table == .env$table_name,
      .data$column_label == .env$column_label,
      .data$row_label == .env$row_label
    ) %>%
    dplyr::pull(value_pct) %>%
    scales::percent(accuracy = accuracy)
}

  plotting_tables$existing$walk %>%
    dplyr::filter(table == "walk_duration_summary", minutes == competitive_minute_label) %>%

    dplyr::mutate(mode = "bike"),
  plotting_tables$existing$transit %>%
    dplyr::filter(table == "transit_duration_summary", minutes == competitive_minute_label) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(mode = "transit"),
  plotting_tables$compare_all_four %>%
    dplyr::filter(scenario == "base", minutes == competitive_minute_label) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(mode = "overall")
) %>%
  dplyr::select(mode, row_label, value_pct)

summary_percent <- function(mode, row_label, accuracy = 2) {
  competitive_percentages %>%
    dplyr::filter(.data$mode == .env$mode, .data$row_label == .env$row_label) %>%
    dplyr::pull(value_pct) %>%
    scales::percent(accuracy = accuracy)
}

scenario_percentages <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  plotting_tables$potential,
  function(scenario_data, scenario_key) {
    scenario_data %>%
      dplyr::filter(minutes == competitive_minute_label) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        scenario_key = scenario_key,
        scenario = as.character(scenario)
      )
  }
)

scenario_percent <- function(scenario_key, scenario, row_label, accuracy = 0.1) {
  scenario_percentages %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      .data$scenario_key == .env$scenario_key,
      .data$scenario == .env$scenario,
      .data$row_label == .env$row_label
    ) %>%
    dplyr::pull(value_pct) %>%
    scales::percent(accuracy = accuracy)
}

vmt_target_attainment <- competitive_percentages %>%
  dplyr::filter(mode == "overall", row_label == "% of VMT") %>%
  dplyr::pull(value_pct) / vmt_reduction_target
```

The summary tables below use results for **`r summary_city`**.

In this study, we consider the potential to reduce vehicle miles traveled (VMT) in the Twin Cities
region that might be achieved by incentivizing people to switch from traveling in cars to walking,
biking or riding transit. We do so by estimating the maximum feasible shift of car trips to
alternative modes given existing land-use and travel patterns, as observed in 380,000 real-world
trips reported in the 2019 and 2021 Travel Behavior Inventory (TBI) surveys. For each observed car
trip, we calculate the best available walk path, bike path, and transit path, considering the quality of
the available infrastructure and transit service. We consider an option to be feasible if we observe a
substantial number (5% or more) of people using that mode under similar circumstances, and if the
traveler has sufficient time to complete the trip within their travel schedule. Further, we consider a
feasible option to be competitive if its travel time is within `r competitive_minutes` minutes of the car trip it would replace.
Our analysis also examines which modes can absorb the largest mode shift, as summarized in @fig-feasibility-competitive-mode-shift. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-competitive-mode-shift
#| fig-cap: "Potential to reduce vehicle trips and VMT by shifting car trips to walking, biking or transit"
mode_shift_bars <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  plotting_tables$existing$all_four %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      table == "overall_shifts",
      column_label %in% c(
        "Feasible to switch to walk",
        "Feasible to switch to bike",
        "Feasible to switch to transit"
      )
    ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      mode = dplyr::recode(
        as.character(column_label),
        "Feasible to switch to walk" = "Walk",
        "Feasible to switch to bike" = "Bike",
        "Feasible to switch to transit" = "Transit"
      ),
      status = "Feasible"
    ),
  plotting_tables$existing$walk %>%
    dplyr::filter(table == "walk_duration_summary", minutes == competitive_minute_label) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(mode = "Walk", status = "Competitive"),
  plotting_tables$existing$bike %>%
    dplyr::filter(table == "bike_duration_summary", minutes == competitive_minute_label) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(mode = "Bike", status = "Competitive"),
  plotting_tables$existing$transit %>%
    dplyr::filter(table == "transit_duration_summary", minutes == competitive_minute_label) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(mode = "Transit", status = "Competitive")
) %>%
  dplyr::select(mode, status, row_label, value_pct) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    mode = factor(mode, levels = c("Walk", "Bike", "Transit")),
    status = factor(status, levels = c("Feasible", "Competitive"))
  )

mode_trip_bars <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = dplyr::filter(mode_shift_bars, row_label == "% of Car Trips"),
  x = ~value_pct, y = ~mode, color = ~status,
  colors = c("#b4d17c", "#7cae1b"),
  type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  text = ~paste0(scales::percent(value_pct), " ", status),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
  textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}<br>%{fullData.name}: %{x:.0%}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout(
    subtitle = "Percent of car trips"
  ) %>%
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(tickformat = "1%", range = c(0, 0.6)))

mode_vmt_bars <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = dplyr::filter(mode_shift_bars, row_label == "% of VMT"),
  x = ~value_pct, y = ~mode, color = ~status,
  colors = c("#b7d4ec", colors$councilBlue),
  type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  text = ~paste0(scales::percent(value_pct), " ", status),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
  textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}<br>%{fullData.name}: %{x:.0%}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout(
    subtitle = "Percent of VMT"
  ) %>%

    xaxis = list(tickformat = "1%", range = c(0, 0.6)),

  )

mode_shift_plot <- plotly::subplot(
  mode_trip_bars, mode_vmt_bars,
  shareY = TRUE, margin = 0.06
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout("Feasible and competitive mode shifts under existing conditions") %>%
  plotly::layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h"),
    yaxis = list(autorange = "reversed"),
    yaxis2 = list(autorange = "reversed")
  ) %>%
  plotly::config(responsive = TRUE)
mode_shift_plot
```

Our results show that walking is a competitive alternative for `r summary_percent("walk", "% of Car Trips")` of car trips. However, because
walking is most competitive for short trips, converting these trips to walk would only reduce VMT by
`r summary_percent("walk", "% of VMT")`. Biking is a competitive alternative for `r summary_percent("bike", "% of Car Trips")` of car trips, comprising `r summary_percent("bike", "% of VMT")` of VMT, and transit is
competitive for `r summary_percent("transit", "% of Car Trips")` of car trips, comprising `r summary_percent("transit", "% of VMT")` of VMT. Biking and transit are both feasible options
for much larger share of VMT than walking, but there is a larger gap between feasible and competitive.
This gap highlights the potential to improve the competitiveness of these modes by enabling more
direct bike routes or faster and more frequent transit service.

For some trips, more than one alternative mode is feasible, and in those cases we consider the
competitiveness of the fastest available mode. **Overall, in the selected region today, `r summary_percent("overall", "% of Car Trips")` of
car trips could shift to walk, bike or transit with travel times within `r competitive_minutes` minutes of driving, and
these trips represent `r summary_percent("overall", "% of VMT", accuracy = 0.1)` of VMT.**

<!-- infrastructure and service changes to further encourage mode shifts. To provide a starting point for -->
<!-- those discussions, we evaluated the potential of six very broad scenarios to increase the -->

- Walk infrastructure: it is safe and comfortable to walk everywhere it is legal to do so;
- Bike infrastructure: it is safe and comfortable to bike everywhere it is legal to do so;
- E-bikes: additionally, everyone has an e-bike;
- Transit frequency: transit frequency is doubled for all routes;
- Highway speed: speed limits are reduced based on NACTO guidelines; and
- All of the above.

@fig-scenario-compare-plot shows the results of this scenario analysis, considering the percent of car trips and VMT for
which the fastest feasible alternative in each scenario is within `r competitive_minutes` minutes of the car travel time. The
results show that among the individual scenarios, the e-bike scenario provides a competitive alternative
for the greatest share of VMT, followed by the bike scenario.

# Existing Mode Shift Potential

This section reports the potential for car trips to shift to walk, bike, transit, or any of these modes. It
aims to address the question:

> With land use, transportation system, and travel patterns held constant, how much potential exists for travel to shift from driving towards other, less carbon-intensive modes?

## Potential shift to walk

To measure the possible walk routes, we create an “all
streets” network from OpenStreetMap that includes the
street system and off-street walking paths but excludes
freeways and other facilities where walking is prohibited.
We introduce a penalty to reflect that walkers tend to avoid
roads with a higher walking level of traffic stress (LTS)—
those roads with high speeds, high functional classes, or
without sidewalks—using an approach developed by the
Virginial DOT for project evaluation (Hardy, Bell, and
McCahill 2019). The resulting paths reflect diversions from
these LTS penalties, as shown in Figure 4, where someone
may walk further to avoid a major arterial. We calculate the
travel time along this longer route assuming a 3 mph
walking speed.


Table 1 shows the feasibility constraints for walk, and the
percentage of car trips and VMT that can feasibly switch
according to each constraint. First, the data show that
22.8% of car trips have a walk alternative less than 1.6 miles
long (compared to 95% of observed walking trips). Because
these trips are by definition short, they comprise only 3% of VMT. Separate from the distance
constraint, the data show that people have sufficient time in their schedule to complete 63% of car
trips by walking instead, comprising 57% of VMT. In many cases, the schedule can accommodate
these switches because the trips are the first or the last of the day, allowing travelers to leave earlier or
arrive later at home. For a trip to be feasible, it must be feasible across all the constraints, and we find
that overall, 18% of car trips and 2.2% of VMT could feasibly switch to walking.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-walk-feasibility-table
#| tbl-cap: "Feasibility of shifting car trips to walking"
walk_feasibility_cells <- plotting_tables$existing$walk %>%
  filter(table == "walk_step_summary") %>%
  mutate(
    column_label = factor(column_label, levels = category_order$walk_step_summary),
    row_label = factor(row_label, levels = metric_order)
  ) %>%
  arrange(column_label, row_label)

walk_feasibility_cells %>%
  select(column_label, row_label, value_pct) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = row_label, values_from = value_pct) %>%
  gt::gt(caption = table_titles[["walk_step_summary"]]) %>%
  gt::cols_label(column_label = "Feasibility constraint") %>%
  gt::fmt_percent(columns = all_of(metric_order), decimals = 1) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = table_label_style,
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = column_label == "Feasible across all constraints")
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(style = table_label_style, locations = gt::cells_column_labels()) %>%
  gt::cols_align(
    align = "left",
    columns = tidyselect::where(~ is.character(.x) || is.factor(.x))
  )
```


```{r}
#| label: tbl-walk-duration-table
#| tbl-cap: "Feasible shifts to walking within specific time differences"
walk_duration_cells <- plotting_tables$existing$walk %>%
  filter(table == "walk_duration_summary") %>%
  mutate(
    column_label = factor(minutes, levels = category_order$duration_minutes),

  ) %>%

walk_duration_cells %>%

  gt::gt(caption = table_titles[["walk_duration_summary"]]) %>%
  gt::cols_label(column_label = "Travel time difference (alternative time - drive time)") %>%
  gt::fmt_percent(columns = all_of(metric_order), decimals = 1) %>%
  gt::sub_missing(columns = all_of(metric_order), missing_text = "\u2014") %>%
  gt::tab_style(style = table_label_style, locations = gt::cells_column_labels()) %>%
  gt::cols_align(
    align = "left",

```


## Potential shift to bike 


As with walking, we calculated
bike routes using an “all streets”
network derived from
OpenStreetMap, but filtered to
include all bicycle facilities and
exclude roads where bicycling is
prohibited. Previous research
indicates that bicyclists are highly
averse to riding on busy and high-
speed streets, especially without
bike lanes (Hood et al. 2014;
Broach 2016). To reflect this
aversion, our routing considers
the bicycle level of traffic stress
(LTS) (Furth, Mekuria, and Nixon
2016), as illustrated in Figure 6
and previously used by the
University of Minnesota (Owen and Murphy 2020). We calculate the bike routes by imposing a 10%
penalty for biking on LTS 2 facilities and assuming that bicyclists who encounter LTS 3 and 4 facilities
will dismount and walk their bikes until they reach a more comfortable street or path. While existing
cyclists do sometimes ride on these facilities, a mode shift suggests the need to attract new cyclists
who will be less confident. We also assume bicyclists will avoid hills if it does not make their trip too
much longer. These penalties result in routes that avoid busier facilities, as the example in Figure 7
shows. We assume that bicyclists travel at 12 mph along their preferred route and that it takes 1
minute at either end to lock or unlock a bike.


Table 3 shows the feasibility constraints for bike, and the
percentage of car trips and VMT that can feasibly switch
according to each constraint. Among observed bike
trips, only 5% are longer than 10 miles in length and 67%
of car trips have a preferred bicycle route within this
distance, amounting to 27% of VMT. The TBI data were
collected year-round, allowing us to analyze weather
conditions. We found that fewer than 5% of bicycle trips
are made when snow is on the ground, and 76% of car
trips and VMT are made when there is not snow on the
ground. 87% of car trips and 94% of VMT have a
preferred bicycle route alternative with no more than
15% of the distance on LTS 3 or 4 facilities. People’s
travel schedules have sufficient time to complete 71% of
car trips and 64% of VMT by bike instead. When
considering all four constraints, biking is a feasible
option for 33% of car trips and 13% of VMT.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bike-feasibility-table

    row_label = factor(row_label, levels = metric_order)
  ) %>%
  arrange(column_label, row_label)

bike_feasibility_cells %>%
  select(column_label, row_label, value_pct) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = row_label, values_from = value_pct) %>%
  gt::gt(caption = table_titles[["bike_step_summary"]]) %>%
  gt::cols_label(column_label = "Feasibility constraint") %>%
  gt::fmt_percent(columns = all_of(metric_order), decimals = 1) %>%
  gt::sub_missing(columns = all_of(metric_order), missing_text = "\u2014") %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = table_label_style,
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = column_label == "Feasible across all constraints")
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(style = table_label_style, locations = gt::cells_column_labels()) %>%

    align = "left",
```

## Potential shift to transit

We calculated using a method similar to a smartphone’s
mapping app’s method. The method uses data from the
General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) files published
by Metro Transit and Minnesota Valley Transit Authority
for October 2019. GTFS is a standard format operators
use to publish their schedules for use in mapping apps.
Our routing method considers the exact departure or
arrival time of the trip and reflects the scheduled transit
vehicles and possible transfers available at that time, as well
as the walking time to, from or between transit vehicles.
For trips to work, school, or medical appointments, we
assume the arrival time is fixed and calculate the latest
departure from the trip’s origin that would reach the
destination in time. For other trips, we calculate the
earliest arrival given the departure time. Because the
waiting time and route vary based on the trip’s timing, we
allowed arrivals up to 5 minutes late at work, school, or
medical appointments, and departures up to 5 minutes early for other trips, if they made the trip at
least 15 minutes faster. Figure 9 shows a transit path in Minneapolis.
Table 5 summarizes the feasibility constraints for transit and the percentage of car trips and VMT that
meet each. A valid transit path with 2 or fewer transfers is possible for 61% of car trips, corresponding
to 48% of VMT. Note that we impose the transfer limit (and a loose 1.5-mile limit on walking
distance) in the routing method itself to avoid creating a large number of complex and infeasible paths,
so the subsequent constraints rely on first meeting this constraint. Walking distance to or from a transit
vehicle is also a barrier to using transit and reflects the overall coverage of the bus system. For 48%
of car trips and 37% of VMT, the possible transit path involves walking less than 0.97 miles from the
origin to the first transit stop, and for about the same percentages, the preferred transit path involves
walking less than 0.93 miles from the final transit stop to the destination. For 45% of car trips and
31% of VMT, the possible transit path involves waiting less than 64 minutes for the first vehicle,
implying that a route running 30 minute or better headways would not be constraining. Each of these

```{r}
#| label: tbl-transit-feasibility-table
#| tbl-cap: "Feasibility of shifting car trips to transit"
transit_feasibility_cells <- plotting_tables$existing$transit %>%
  filter(table == "transit_step_summary") %>%
  mutate(
    column_label = factor(column_label, levels = category_order$transit_step_summary),
    row_label = factor(row_label, levels = metric_order)
  ) %>%
```

# Possible Actions to Increase Mode Shift Potential

Above, we examine how many car trips and how much VMT could feasibly and completely shift to
walk, bike or transit assuming land use, the transportation system and travel patterns remain as
currently observed. Next, we build upon that analysis to consider:
> By how much may changes to the transportation system increase the mode shift
potential?


To provide a starting point for discussions about how to effectively increase the mode shift potential,
we evaluated the potential of six very broad scenarios to increase the competitiveness of alternative
modes:

- Walk infrastructure: it is safe and comfortable to walk everywhere it is legal to do so;
- Bike infrastructure: it is safe and comfortable to bike everywhere it is legal to do so;
- E-bikes: additionally, everyone has an e-bike;
- Transit frequency: transit frequency is doubled for all routes;
- Roadway speed: speed limits are reduced based on NACTO guidelines; and
- All of the above.

## Improving walk infrastructure

The street environment affects people’s comfort and safety when walking. Most people would rather
walk along a sidewalk on a quiet street than along a busy road with traffic speeding past. In this study,
we reflect those preferences by selecting walking routes that are weighted to avoid higher class and
higher speed streets. This scenario imagines a region where every street is safe and comfortable to
walk along. This ideal environment includes sidewalks everywhere, speed limits no more than 30 mph,
and roads no wider than four lanes. People would walk the shortest distance to their destination,
saving travel time.

@fig-scenario-walk-plot shows the results of this scenario, compared to the existing conditions. It focuses on
competitive shifts, where a competitive shift must be feasible and provide a travel time close to driving.
It shows the percentage of car trips that can competitively shift to walking within
`r paste(category_order$duration_minutes, collapse = ", ")` of the travel time of driving. It also shows the percentage of VMT that these car
trips comprise. The results show that improving walk infrastructure would increase the
competitiveness of walking slightly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scenario-walk-plot
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of car trips and VMT that can competitively shift to walking for a scenario where walking is safe and comfortable on all streets"
walk_scenario_cells <- plotting_tables$potential$best_walk %>%
  mutate(
    scenario = factor(
      recode(
        as.character(scenario),
        base = "Existing conditions",
        best_walk = scenario_headings[["best_walk"]]
      ),
      levels = c("Existing conditions", scenario_headings[["best_walk"]])
    ),
    column_label = factor(minutes, levels = category_order$duration_minutes),
    row_label = factor(row_label, levels = metric_order)
  ) %>%
  arrange(column_label, row_label, scenario)


walk_scenario_trips <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = filter(walk_scenario_cells, row_label == "% of Car Trips"),
  x = ~value_pct,
  y = ~column_label,
  color = ~scenario,
  colors = c(
    report_colors[["Existing conditions: % of Car Trips"]],
    report_colors[["Scenario: % of Car Trips"]]
  ),
  type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  text = ~ scales::percent(value_pct),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
  textposition = "outside",
  customdata = ~ as.character(column_label), hovertemplate = plot_hover_template
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout(
    subtitle = "% of Car Trips"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis = list(
      tickformat = "1%",
      range = c(0, 0.6)
    )
  )


walk_scenario_vmt <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = filter(walk_scenario_cells, row_label == "% of VMT"),
  x = ~value_pct,
  y = ~column_label,
  color = ~scenario,
  colors = c(
    report_colors[["Existing conditions: % of VMT"]],
    report_colors[["Scenario: % of VMT"]]
  ),
  type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  text = ~ scales::percent(value_pct),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
  textposition = "outside",
  customdata = ~ as.character(column_label), hovertemplate = plot_hover_template
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout(
    subtitle = "% of VMT"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis = list(
      tickformat = "1%",
      range = c(0, 0.6)
    )
  )


walk_scenario_plot <- plotly::subplot(
  walk_scenario_trips, walk_scenario_vmt,
  shareY = TRUE, margin = 0.06
) %>%
  plotly_layout("Competitve shift to walk in walk improvement scenario") %>%
  layout(
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      xaxis = list(tickformat = "1%")
    ),
    yaxis = list(autorange = "reversed"),
    yaxis2 = list(autorange = "reversed")
  )
walk_scenario_plot
```

## Improving bike infrastructure

Many bicyclists are reluctant to ride on busy roads due to safety concerns and the stress of being near
traffic. We reflect this reluctance by selecting bike routes that avoid roads with a high Level of Traffic
Stress (LTS). This scenario imagines a region where everyone can safely and
comfortably bike on any street. We represent this scenario by coding all streets except freeways with
LTS 1, reflecting the best possible biking conditions. Bicyclists would therefore save travel time on
each trip, because they could take the most direct route to their destination, without diverting or
dismounting to avoid busy streets.


@fig-scenario-bike-plot shows results of this scenario, compared to existing conditions. Under this scenario,
many more car trips could feasibly shift to biking and maintain competitive travel times across all
three time thresholds. At a `r competitive_minutes`-minute travel time difference, the share of car trips that could shift to biking increases from `r scenario_percent("best_bike", "base", "% of Car Trips")` to `r scenario_percent("best_bike", "best_bike", "% of Car Trips")`, while the share of VMT increases from `r scenario_percent("best_bike", "base", "% of VMT")` to `r scenario_percent("best_bike", "best_bike", "% of VMT")`. Biking holds a high potential as an alternative to driving, but the
quality of the existing bike infrastructure in the Twin Cities region is a major barrier to achieving that
potential.

## Universal e-bikes

In the past few years, e-bikes have become more widely available and popular. The battery-electric
motor on an e-bike reduces the effort required to pedal, improves acceleration, and increases the
average speed. It therefore makes biking easier and faster. In this scenario, we build upon the bike
scenario described above and imagine that in addition to the bike infrastructure improvements,
everyone has access to an e-bike. We represent this change by increasing the biking speed by 13%,
and removing avoidance of steep hills.

@fig-scenario-ebike-plot shows results. Within `r competitive_minutes` minutes of driving, `r scenario_percent("e_bike", "e_bike", "% of Car Trips", accuracy = 1)` of car trips and `r scenario_percent("e_bike", "e_bike", "% of VMT", accuracy = 1)` of VMT could feasibly shift to e-biking.

## Double transit frequency

Traveling by public transit incurs travel time in several parts. The traveler must walk to the stop, wait
for the bus or train, ride to another stop, and walk to their destination. Trips that require a transfer
involve another walking and waiting step. Therefore, there are several ways to improve the
competitiveness of transit: by adding stops closer to the desired origins and destinations (increasing
coverage), by increasing the speed of the transit vehicles (such as through exclusive bus lanes or
limited-stop service), or by reducing waiting times through increased service frequency. In this
scenario, we focus on the latter, and imagine a region in which the same transit routes are operated at
double their current frequency. Thus, a route that currently runs twice per hour would instead run
four times per hour, reducing the average headway from 30 minutes to 15 minutes, saving travelers
up to 15 minutes of waiting time, depending on when they depart. Travelers may also select different
paths, particularly if the shorter waiting times open more opportunities for transfers.

@fig-scenario-transit-plot shows the effect of doubling transit frequencies. Within `r competitive_minutes` minutes of driving, the share of car trips that could shift to transit increases from `r scenario_percent("double_transit", "base", "% of Car Trips")` to `r scenario_percent("double_transit", "double_transit", "% of Car Trips")`; the share of VMT increases from `r scenario_percent("double_transit", "base", "% of VMT")` to `r scenario_percent("double_transit", "double_transit", "% of VMT")`.


## Reduce roadway speeds

The competitiveness of more sustainable modes depends both on the feasibility and travel times of
those modes, and on the travel time to drive. Therefore, it is also possible to increase the
competitiveness of other modes by reducing driving speeds with lower speed limits and/or street
designs that naturally limit the driving speed. Here, we consider a scenario where the travel speeds on
all streets in the Twin Cities region are adjusted to be consistent with guidance from the National
Association of City Transportation Officials (NACTO). As a complement to the American
Association of State Highway and Transportation Official’s (AASHTO’s) “green book”, NACTO
publishes street design guidance focused on serving the mix of car, walk, bike and transit users found
in urban and suburban areas (NACTO 2013). Their current guidance for urban areas (NACTO 2020)
suggests:

- 10 mph on shared streets and alleys,
- 20 mph on minor streets,
- 25 mph on major streets, with a variation of up to 25 mph for streets in low density areas with
well-protected places for people to walk and bike.


We apply the 10-mph limit to shared streets and alleys and the 20-mph limit to locals and collectors.
In urban areas, we apply a 25-mph speed limit to arterials, and 25 mph in suburban areas. In addition,
we limit freeway speeds to 55 mph in urban areas and 70 mph in suburban and rural areas. We
represent these changes in a scenario by limiting travel speeds on those types of facilities to no more
than the values indicated, assuming the streets are designed such that drivers comply. In both the
base case and the scenario, we set the free flow travel speed (excluding congestion) to 80% of the
speed limit to account acceleration and deceleration time from intersections.

@fig-scenario-speed-plot shows the results of this road speed scenario, compared to existing conditions. It shows
that these changes would slightly increase the competitiveness of switching to any non-car mode.
There are two ways to view the modest changes resulting from this scenario: that these specific road
speed changes provide limited benefit in terms of increasing the mode shift potential, or that they can
be implemented with limited cost to those who currently drive. Further, these road speed changes
would provide other benefits. First, they would improve the walking and biking conditions and would
therefore likely be necessary to implement the walk and bike scenarios described above. Second, they
would have safety benefits, with research showing that reducing roadway speeds can reduce both total
crashes and fatal and serious injury crashes (NACTO 2020).

```{r}
#| label: fig-scenario-speed-plot
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of car trips and VMT that can competitively shift to walking, biking or transit for a scenario where roadway speeds are limited based on NACTO guidelines"
speed_scenario_cells <- plotting_tables$potential$slow_car %>%
  mutate(
    scenario = factor(
      recode(
        as.character(scenario),
        base = "Existing conditions",
        slow_car = scenario_headings[["slow_car"]]
      ),
      levels = c("Existing conditions", scenario_headings[["slow_car"]])
    ),
    column_label = factor(minutes, levels = category_order$duration_minutes),
    row_label = factor(row_label, levels = metric_order)
  ) %>%
  arrange(column_label, row_label, scenario)
speed_scenario_trips <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = filter(speed_scenario_cells, row_label == "% of Car Trips"),
  x = ~value_pct, y = ~column_label, color = ~scenario,
  colors = c(
    report_colors[["Existing conditions: % of Car Trips"]],
    report_colors[["Scenario: % of Car Trips"]]
  ),
  type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  text = ~ scales::percent(value_pct),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
  textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  customdata = ~ as.character(column_label), hovertemplate = plot_hover_template
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout(subtitle = "% of Car Trips") %>%
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(tickformat = "1%", range = c(0, 0.6)))


speed_scenario_vmt <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = filter(speed_scenario_cells, row_label == "% of VMT"),
  x = ~value_pct, y = ~column_label, color = ~scenario,
  colors = c(
    report_colors[["Existing conditions: % of VMT"]],
    report_colors[["Scenario: % of VMT"]]
  ),
  type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  text = ~ scales::percent(value_pct),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
  textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  customdata = ~ as.character(column_label), hovertemplate = plot_hover_template
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout(subtitle = "% of VMT") %>%
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(tickformat = "1%", range = c(0, 0.6)))

speed_scenario_plot <- plotly::subplot(
  speed_scenario_trips, speed_scenario_vmt,
  shareY = TRUE, margin = 0.06
) %>%
  plotly_layout("Competitve shift to any non-car mode in reduced roadway speed scenario") %>%
  plotly::layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h"),
    yaxis = list(autorange = "reversed"),
    yaxis2 = list(autorange = "reversed")
  )
speed_scenario_plot
```

## All of the above

More than one of the above scenarios could be implemented together, and they may be
complementary. Limiting roadway speeds would also improve the walk and bike environment of
many streets, and improvements to the walk and bike environment may be mutually beneficial. Here,
we envision an all of the above scenario, where every street is safe and comfortable for both walking
and biking, everyone has access to an e-bike, transit frequency is doubled throughout the region, and
roadway speeds are limited consistent with NACTO guidance.

@fig-scenario-combined-plot shows the mode shift potential for this scenario, compared to existing conditions. Within `r competitive_minutes` minutes of driving, the share of car trips that could shift to a non-car mode increases from `r scenario_percent("all_four", "base", "% of Car Trips")` to `r scenario_percent("all_four", "all_four", "% of Car Trips")`; the share of VMT increases from `r scenario_percent("all_four", "base", "% of VMT")` to `r scenario_percent("all_four", "all_four", "% of VMT")`.

```{r}

#| fig-cap: "Percentage of car trips and VMT that can competitively shift to walking, biking or transit for a scenario where all of the above improvements are implemented"
combined_scenario_cells <- plotting_tables$potential$all_four %>%
  mutate(
    scenario = factor(
      recode(
        as.character(scenario),
        base = "Existing conditions",

      ),
      levels = c("Existing conditions", scenario_headings[["all_four"]])
    ),
    column_label = factor(minutes, levels = category_order$duration_minutes),
    row_label = factor(row_label, levels = metric_order)
  ) %>%

combined_scenario_trips <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = filter(combined_scenario_cells, row_label == "% of Car Trips"),
  x = ~value_pct, y = ~column_label, color = ~scenario,

  ),

  text = ~ scales::percent(value_pct),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
  textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  customdata = ~ as.character(column_label), hovertemplate = plot_hover_template
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout(subtitle = "% of Car Trips") %>%
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(tickformat = "1%", range = c(0, 0.6)))


combined_scenario_vmt <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = filter(combined_scenario_cells, row_label == "% of VMT"),
```

## Scenario comparison

@fig-scenario-compare-plot compares the results of each scenario, focusing on feasible shifts from car to any other
mode that has a travel time within `r competitive_minutes` minutes of driving. All scenarios would increase the
competitiveness of non-car modes, with the bike scenario providing the largest individual effect, and
the all of the above scenario providing the largest overall effect.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scenario-compare-plot
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of car trips and VMT that can feasibly shift to walking, biking or transit with travel times within 15 minutes of driving for transportation improvement scenarios"


compare_scen_cells <- plotting_tables$compare_all_four %>%
  mutate(
    scenario = recode_factor(
        as.character(scenario),
        base = "Existing conditions",
        best_walk = "Walk Scenario",
        best_bike = "Bike Scenario",
        e_bike = "E-Bike Scenario",
        double_transit = "Transit Scenario",
        slow_car = "Road Speed Scenario",
        all_four = "All of the Above Scenario",
        .ordered = TRUE,
        
      ),
      # levels = c("Existing conditions", "Walk Scenario", "Bike Scenario", "E-Bike Scenario", "Transit Scenario", "Road Speed Scenario", "All of the Above Scenario"),
      # ordered = TRUE
    column_label = factor(minutes, levels = category_order$duration_minutes),
    row_label = factor(row_label, levels = metric_order)
  ) %>%
  arrange(column_label, row_label, scenario)




compare_scenario_trips <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = filter(compare_scen_cells, row_label == "% of Car Trips"),
  x = ~value_pct, y = ~scenario,
  type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  name = "% of Car Trips",
  text = ~ scales::percent(value_pct),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
    marker = list(color = colors$councilBlue,
                fill = colors$councilBlue),
  textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  customdata = ~ as.character(column_label), hovertemplate = plot_hover_template
) %>%
  councilR::plotly_layout(subtitle = "% of Car Trips") %>%
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(tickformat = "1%", range = c(0, 0.6)))


compare_scenario_vmt <- plotly::plot_ly(
  data = filter(compare_scen_cells, row_label == "% of VMT"),
  x = ~value_pct, y = ~scenario,
  type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  text = ~ scales::percent(value_pct),
  textfont = list(family = "Arial Narrow"),
  marker = list(color = colors$councilBlue,
                fill = colors$councilBlue),
  name = "% of VMT",
  textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
```
